message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute or question, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it cannot exceed **two months’ rent** for a month‑to‑month lease or **one month’s rent** for a fixed‑term lease.
• The landlord must return the deposit within **30 days** after you move out, unless they provide a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs you made.
• Request the deposit return in writing and keep a copy. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas law requires landlords to maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition.
• Landlords must repair major problems (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural issues) within a reasonable time after notice. | • Document problems with photos and written notice.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but do so only after following the proper procedure. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: the lease ends automatically unless you give notice to renew or the landlord gives notice to terminate. | • Keep a copy of any notice you send or receive. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the formal eviction process: serve a **notice to vacate** (usually 30 days for nonpayment, 10 days for other violations).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord files an unlawful detainer action in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a counterclaim or seek a stay of eviction. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | • Never sign a new lease or addendum without reading it fully. | | **Utilities & Services** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord approval. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division.
• Texas Commission on Human Rights.
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union).
• HUD’s Fair Housing website. | • Use these resources for disputes, complaints, or legal assistance. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on rent, deposits, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask for a copy of the lease** – keep a signed copy for your records. 3. **Verify the landlord’s identity** – confirm they own the property or have written permission to lease. 4. **Check for habitability disclosures** – the landlord must disclose known lead paint hazards, mold, or other health risks. 5. **Confirm security deposit limits** – ensure it does not exceed the statutory maximum. 6. **Ask about utility responsibilities** – clarify which utilities you will pay. --- #### When You’re Facing a Problem | Issue | First Step | Where to Seek Help | |-------|------------|--------------------| | Landlord refuses to return deposit | Send a written demand letter | Texas Attorney General, local tenant‑rights group | | Landlord fails to repair a major issue | File a written complaint with the landlord | Texas Attorney General, local code enforcement | | Eviction notice received | Respond in writing, request a hearing | Texas Courts, legal aid | | Discrimination claim | File a complaint with HUD or Texas Commission on Human Rights | HUD website, Texas Commission on Human Rights | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have statutory protections against unfair deposits, unsafe living conditions, unreasonable eviction practices, and discrimination. Keep detailed records, communicate in writing, and use the available state and federal resources if you encounter problems.

There's no request for generating a contract. So we don't need to call the function. Just answer. Provide overview: security deposit, habitability, notice, eviction, etc. Also mention resources. Provide citations? Not necessary. Just give a thorough answer.
